title: Modelling Tables as Data
narrative:
The `TableData` value is SwingTree's answer to the question
    "where does the data of my table live?".

    It is a single immutable value describing an entire table: its cells, the name
    and class of every column, the cell order tying the two together, and whether
    the user may edit any of it. You hold one
    in a property, you bind that property to a table, and from then on your business
    logic never touches Swing again - it merely produces the next version of a value.

    Because it is a value, it is thread safe by construction: the application thread
    and the UI thread can hand it to each other without locks. And because its cells
    live in `Tuple`s, which remember how they were derived from their predecessor,
    a table bound to it updates *incrementally* rather than rebuilding itself.

features.id: A table is built up out of columns and rows, and reads back the way you wrote it.

extraInfo:
The usual way of building a table is to name its columns first and then
            to pour rows into it. Note how the row values are plain objects: you do
            not have to wrap anything.

blocks.text: A table with three named columns and two rows.
It has the dimensions you would expect.
Every cell reads back in plain (row, column) terms.
The columns know their names, and you may look them up by name.
You may also read whole rows and columns at once.

features.id: A table is a value, so changing it never touches the table you started with.

extraInfo:
Every method which sounds like it changes something really returns a *new*
            `TableData`. This is what makes the whole thing thread safe, and it is also
            what lets a table tell whether anything actually changed: two tables with
            the same columns and cells are equal to each other.

blocks.text: A table, and a second one built exactly the same way.
The two are equal and agree on their hash code.
We derive a new table by changing a cell...
...the original is left exactly as it was.
A change which changes nothing hands you back the very same table.
So does a change which is out of bounds.

features.id: The empty table is empty, and is where a table without columns starts.

blocks.text: It has nothing in it, no matter how you ask.
A table with columns but no rows is still empty, because it has nothing to show.
But it does know about its columns, which is what a table header needs.

features.id: A table can be described completely, in a single call, through the full `TableData.of(..)` factory.

extraInfo:
A table is made of five things: the cells, the column names, the column
            classes, the cell order and the editability. The short `TableData.of(..)`
            factories only take some of these and fill in defaults for the rest. This
            longer one takes all five.

            Use it when you already hold the whole description, for example after parsing
            a file or reading a server response. It saves you from building the table up
            one column at a time.

blocks.text: A complete description of a small, editable, row major table.
Each of the five things we spelled out reads straight back off the table.
Its two dimensions follow from the cells, so there is nothing to keep in sync by hand.
The column classes are what a `JTable` consults to pick its renderers and editors.

features.id: Rows can be added, replaced and removed, one at a time or in ranges.

extraInfo:
Range operations are not just a convenience, they are the efficient path:
            a row major table hands a range change to a `JTable` as a *single* event,
            so adding a hundred rows repaints once rather than a hundred times.

blocks.text: A table with two columns and three rows.
We insert a row in the middle...
...it lands exactly where we asked.
We add several rows at once...
...they are all appended, in order.
We replace a range of rows...
...only that range changed.
We remove a range of rows...
...only the survivors remain.
We remove every row...
...the columns stay behind, ready to be filled again.

features.id: Columns can be added and removed, taking their names and classes along.

extraInfo:
A column is not just a strip of cells, it also has a name and a class
            (which is what a `JTable` consults to pick a renderer). So adding or
            removing one moves all three together, and you never have to keep a
            separate list of headers in sync by hand.

blocks.text: A table with two columns and two rows.
We append a column...
...the table grew a column, with its name, class and cells all in place.
The rows we already had are still intact.
We insert a column in the middle instead...
...everything to its right shifts over.
We remove a column...
...its name and cells go with it.
We replace the cells of a column...
...only that column changed.

features.id: A column inserted into a column major table lines its cells up with its header.

extraInfo:
The column metadata of a table takes part in deciding how wide it is,
            so a column major table may well describe more columns than its cells
            tuple holds lines for. Inserting a column into such a table must place
            the new cells under the inserted header, and not under whichever column
            happens to hold cells already.

blocks.text: A column major table whose two columns exist only as metadata so far.
We insert a column, with cells, between the two...
...the new cells sit exactly under the new header...
...while the metadata only columns to its left and right stay empty.
A row major table built the very same way agrees on every single cell.

features.id: A table can be reshaped fundamentally: its rows, columns and types may all change.

extraInfo:
Nothing about the shape of a `TableData` is fixed once and for all. The
            same property can hold a two column table of strings now and a four column
            table of numbers and booleans a moment later. This matters because real
            applications do exactly this: you switch a report, you pivot a view, you
            load a different file.

blocks.text: A modest table of two string columns.
It starts out as plain untyped columns.
We reshape it completely: new columns, new names, new classes, new rows.
It is a different table entirely, and it knows its new types.
The cells are the new ones.
The table we started with never noticed any of it.

features.id: The class of a column can change on the fly, which is how a table changes its renderers.

blocks.text: A table whose single column is untyped.
It starts out as a plain object column.
We tell it that the column really holds booleans...
...it says so, which is what makes a JTable draw check boxes for it.
Setting the class it already has hands back the very same table.

features.id: A table can be made editable (or read only) without touching a cell.

extraInfo:
Whether the user may edit the cells is a property of the table value, so
            flipping it is a change of the value like any other. Because editability is
            separate from the cell order, flipping it can never disturb how the cells
            are read. Note that a table also has to live in a mutable `Var` before an
            edit has anywhere to go.

blocks.text: A read only table.
It does not permit editing.
We make it editable...
...it does, and not a single cell moved.
Its cell order came through untouched.
Asking for the editability it already has hands back the very same table.
Making it read only again gives us back an equal table.

features.id: A column major table speaks in rows and columns just like a row major one.

extraInfo:
The cell order only decides how the cells are *stored*. Everything else on this
            class talks in `(row, column)` terms regardless, so a column major table
            grows a row just as happily as a row major one does - it is merely a little
            more work for it internally, which is one reason to prefer row major for
            large tables.

blocks.text: The very same cells, read once as rows and once as columns.
They are different values, because they show different tables.
The same cells are transposed between the two.
We add a row to the column major table...
...it lands as a row, exactly as it would have in a row major table.
And when we remove a column from it...
...that works out too.

features.id: Changing the cell order of a table reinterprets its cells, which transposes what it shows.

extraInfo:
The cell order says how the cells are *stored*, not how they are displayed.
            Changing it therefore moves no cells at all. It only changes which axis the
            outer `Tuple` is read along, which means the same cells come out transposed.

            Use `withCellOrder(..)` when the cells were the other way around all along.
            It is not a way to flip a table on screen.

blocks.text: A row major table of two rows, three cells wide, which the user may edit.
It reads as the two by three table you would expect.
We declare the very same cells to be stored column by column instead...
...the table turns onto its side: three rows of two cells each.
Nothing actually moved, the cells are literally the ones we handed in.
Editability is a separate matter, so it came through the change untouched.
Asking for the cell order it already has hands back the very same table.

features.id: The cell order and the editability of a table are two independent axes. [0]

extraInfo:
Cell order and editability are two separate things. `cellOrder()` says how
            the cells are stored, `editability()` says whether the user may change them.
            Changing one never changes the other.

            That is exactly why they are two enums instead of one: turning editing on
            cannot transpose your table by accident.

blocks.text: A table of two rows, built with the given cell order and editability.
It reports both axes exactly as we asked for them.
The two enums answer the same questions the table does.
We flip the editability over to the other constant...
...only that axis changed, the cell order stayed exactly where it was.
And because no cell was touched, the table still shows what it showed before.
We flip the editability in both directions, in both cell orders.

features.id: A ragged table reads as though its holes were filled with nulls.

extraInfo:
You are not forced to keep every row the same width. A table is as wide as
            its widest row (or as its column metadata, whichever says more), and the
            cells nobody filled in simply read as `null`.

blocks.text: A deliberately ragged table.
It is as wide as its widest row.
The holes read as null, rather than throwing at you.
Reading a whole row pads it out to the width of the table.

features.id: Naming more columns than the cells fill widens the table.

extraInfo:
The column metadata takes part in deciding how wide a table is, which is
            exactly what lets a table have columns but no rows. It also means that
            naming a column nobody has filled in yet simply adds an empty column.

blocks.text: A table with one filled column, but three names.
It is three columns wide, the last two of them empty.
The names are all there.

features.id: A table has a string representation which tells you what it holds.

blocks.text: A small table.
It describes itself usefully.

extraInfo:

The table starts out mirroring the data.
We apply the given reshaping to the property...

features.id: A bound table syncs a range of rows through a single, targeted event.

extraInfo:
This is the pay off of the whole design: because a `Tuple` remembers how it
            was derived, adding a range of rows arrives at the `JTable` as *one*
            insertion of a range, not as a rebuild and not as one event per row.
            This is why you should not worry about the performance of a big table.

blocks.text: A property holding a table of three rows, bound to a JTable.
A listener recording the table model events in a readable form.
code: events << "${e.type == TableModelEvent.INSERT ? 'INSERT' : e.type == TableModelEvent.DELETE ? 'DELETE' : e.type == TableModelEvent.UPDATE ? 'UPDATE' : '?'}[${e.firstRow}..${e.lastRow}]".toString()

blocks.text: We add two rows in one go...
...the table hears about it exactly once, as a range.
We remove a range of rows...
...that too is a single event.
